Tell us about your work

Have you published an article or report, written a thesis, given a talk, or built something with the Active Attack Data? Send us the details and we will list it here. The button opens an email with the questions filled in; a title and a link are enough to start.

title: More Data
text:
Two datasets built from the Active Attack Data: the doors attackers met in K-12 school attacks, and the officers shot in active shooter incidents.
Each comes as CSV files with a PDF codebook, in the same form as the Active Attack Data. Jump to K-12 door security or Officers shot.

title: More Data
text:
K-12 door security
U.S. K-12 active shooter attacks and the doors the attackers came up against: whether each door was locked, barricaded, or breached, and how the attacker got through.



54Attacks66Doors2001–2025Years2025Version





Two CSV files and a PDF codebook
The codebook describes every variable in both files: what it records, its values, and how often it is missing.

 Events (CSV)   Doors (CSV)   Codebook (PDF) 






Two files
The events file has one row per attack (54 rows, 69 variables): school, timing, victims by location, attackers, firearms, and the response. The doors file has one row per door (66 doors in 22 attacks, 26 variables).


Linking them
The files share one column, case_number. To look at doors by an event characteristic, such as school level, join the events file to the doors file on case_number.


Doors
Each door is recorded as coded and grouped as in the 2026 report: lock type, status (locked, unlocked, propped), breach attempts, barricades, whether the attacker got through, and by what route.


Funding and report
Collection of the 2001–2025 data was funded by the Security Industry Association and first reported in ALERRT’s The Role of Locked Doors and Access Control in School-Based Active Shooter Events (2026). Where this version differs from the report, this version is the corrected one.



Suggested citation



Advanced Law Enforcement Rapid Response Training (ALERRT) Center. (2026). K-12 Door Security Dataset (Version 2025) [Data set]. Texas State University. https://activeattackdata.org/datasets.html#k-12-door-security


For the 2001–2025 findings, please also cite the 2026 report.

title: More Data
text:
Officers shot
Law enforcement officers struck by gunfire during active shooter incidents: where they were, how they were hit, and what they were doing at the time.



156Officers75Incidents35Killed2001–2025Years2025Version





A CSV file and a PDF codebook
The codebook describes every variable, the rules for who counts as shot, and the sources behind the coding.

 Data (CSV)   Codebook (PDF) 






One row per officer
156 officers in 75 incidents, 42 variables. Officers shot in the same incident share a case_id; incident-level columns repeat on each officer’s row.


Who counts as shot
An officer is included when struck by gunfire: wounds and grazes, rounds stopped by body armor or equipment, bullet fragments and ricochets, and fire from other officers (blue_on_blue). Injuries only from glass or debris are not counted. The codebook gives the full rules.


Linked to the Active Attack Data
aad_case_code matches case_code in the Active Attack Data, so incident details (location, attacker, casualties) can be joined in. Officer details come from news and agency reports, prosecutor and court records, and FBI LEOKA.


Reading the file
Read officer_id as text: officer 30.10 is not 30.1, and spreadsheet programs will merge them. Officers are named where their names were released; attackers are never named, and the notes say “the attacker” instead.



Suggested citation



Advanced Law Enforcement Rapid Response Training (ALERRT) Center. (2026). Officers Shot in Active Shooter Incidents (Version 2025) [Data set]. Texas State University. https://activeattackdata.org/datasets.html#officers-shot

title: Contact
text:
Questions about the Active Attack Data, this website, or a name on the Remembrance page? Write to either of us.
We are the two members of the ALERRT Center’s research team who maintain the data and this site.

title: Contact
text:
What to write about


The data
Questions about how an attack is defined and counted, what a variable means, or how the figures were produced. The full dataset and codebook are on the Active Attacks page.


A correction
A name missing or wrong on the Remembrance page, or an error in a figure or number. Please tell us the attack’s date and location and, for a name, the source you are working from.


Using the data
If you use the data in research, reporting, or training, we are glad to hear about it. Please credit the ALERRT Center’s Active Attack Data and link to activeattackdata.org.

title: Contact
text:
More from ALERRT
The ALERRT Center at Texas State University trains first responders for active attacks, and its research team studies how these events unfold. Research publications and projects are at ALERRTResearch.org; training at ALERRT.org. The code behind this site is on GitHub.

title: Remembrance
text:
Remembrance
1,434 names of the 1,477 people killed in active attacks in the United States, 2000 to 2025.
Let us pause to remember them, and to honor with courage and compassion their families and those who risked their lives to save others. We try to record every name we can find, but not everyone could be named, so a year’s names can differ from the number of people killed in the data. If a name is missing or wrong, please tell us.

Don’t Name Them
At ALERRT, it is our policy not to name the people responsible for active attacks. Research shows that many attacks are driven by a search for fame; by refusing to name attackers, we aim to remove fame and notoriety as a motive for future attacks. Learn more at DontNameThem.org.

title: Codebook
text:
Every variable in the Active Attack Data, version 2025: what it records, its values, and how often it is missing.
The data have one row per attack, 634 attacks from 2000 through 2025, in 46 variables. Counts below are from this version of the data. Download the data and this codebook on the Active Attacks page.

title: Codebook
text:
How to read the data


What counts as an active attack
An active attack occurs when an individual or individuals is actively killing or attempting to kill multiple unrelated people in a public space. The key word is actively: events that law enforcement learns of only after they end are excluded. Any weapon counts.


Attacker variables
Age, sex, and race carry a suffix for each attacker (age_1, age_2, age_3). For an attack with one attacker, the _2 and _3 variables are empty. The order is arbitrary.


Inclusive counts
Variables ending in _incl use the FBI’s more inclusive definition. ALERRT counts only people shot, wounded, or killed by the attacker; an injury suffered while fleeing is not in wound_tot.


Versions
Version 2025 was released September 8, 2026 and corrected November 6, 2026. Every change is listed under Updates on the Home page.

title: Active Attack Data Explorer
text:
About the data

An active attack occurs when an individual or individuals is actively killing or attempting to kill multiple unrelated people in a public space.

The key word is actively. The definition excludes events that law enforcement learns of only after they end, such as many family annihilations in a private home; first responders are typically alerted to an active attack while it is happening. Even so, more than half of these attacks end before law enforcement arrives, because civilians stop the attacker or the attacker stops (flees or dies by suicide). Any weapon counts, whether a firearm, a knife, or a vehicle, as long as the intent is to kill as many people as possible.
ALERRT began collecting data on active shooter events in 2010 to understand how they unfold and to inform its training, and in 2013 joined the FBI to form an Active Shooter Working Group that supports the FBI’s annual reports. Around 2018 the definition widened from firearms to any weapon, and the data became the Active Attack Data: every FBI-documented firearm attack, plus the non-firearm attacks identified by ALERRT’s research team.
For how “active attack” differs from terms often used in the media, see Sandel & Martaindale (2022), What Are We Talking About? Definitional Confusion Within Active and Mass Shooting Research, Journal of Mass Violence Research.
More about the ALERRT Center’s research at ALERRTResearch.org and its training at ALERRT.org. Questions about the data: see Contact.

title: Active Attack Data Explorer
text:
Updates

11/10/26 - New More Data page with two datasets built from the Active Attack Data: K-12 door security (54 school attacks and the 66 doors the attackers came up against) and officers shot (156 officers struck by gunfire in 75 active shooter incidents). Each comes as CSV with a PDF codebook and a suggested citation.
11/09/26 - New Publications page: the research, reports, and books that used the Active Attack Data, with a button to tell us about work of your own so we can list it.
11/09/26 - New memorial video on the Remembrance page: 1080p, the names rolling by year with officer and under-18 marked, playable on the page and downloadable.
11/09/26 - Added a light/dark switch (the half-moon icon in the top bar). It changes the whole site, and every figure, map, interactive plot, and animation has a dark version drawn for it; downloads give you the version on screen. Also added a Codebook page and PDF built from the data (the Word codebook is retired), a suggested citation, and a redesigned Download the Data tab: download buttons first, a table that pages and scrolls sideways, and links to the v2024 and v2023 files for reproducing earlier work. The Contact page now carries our Texas State email addresses.
11/06/26 - Redesigned the site: a new home page, a header with key numbers on each Active Attacks tab, figures restyled with one color per tab, a fixed count on the state map (Delaware, which has no recorded attacks, had been shown with one), and interactive plots that fit any screen.
11/06/26 - Redesigned the Fact Sheet tab and the downloadable fact sheet PDF. Both now show each figure for 2025 next to 2024 and the 2020–2024 average, add a map of where the 2025 attacks happened, and are built directly from the data. The numbers themselves are unchanged.
11/06/26 - Corrected the “relationship” variable in the downloadable data: 33 attacks by former employees had been coded as “other” instead of “coworker” (coworker is now 99 attacks, other 7). The relationship figures on the Active Attacks page are updated to match. The “location_primary” variable now also carries separate “Church” and “Military base” levels, previously pooled into “other”; the figures still group them with other locations. The codebook has been updated to reflect both changes.
09/14/26 - Moved medical facilities (e.g., hospitals) into the “Business” location type so that the website matches the fact sheet. The “location_primary” variable in the downloadable data now carries a separate “Medical facility” level; these events were previously pooled into “other”. The codebook has also been updated to reflect the change.



Show earlier updates


09/09/26 - Added a link to the Research Ring website.
09/08/26 - Update to v2025 data. The downloadable fact sheet is now a .pdf.
12/04/25 - Added “fact sheet” tab and downloadable fact sheet to the Active Attacks page.
08/29/25 - Changed the section title “fatalities” to “casualties” and added information on the number of wounded.
08/27/25 - Gradient color schemes were removed from plots to avoid double encoding of attack counts/percentages.
06/20/25 - Disaggregated the “Business” category of the “location_primary” variable in the downloadable data. The original category is now split into three: office, factory/warehouse, and retail. The codebook has also been updated to reflect the change.
06/12/25 - Update to v2024 data.
01/23/25 - Initial launch of the Active Attack Data Explorer (v2023).
